intro: France is a republic with a powerful elected president, a two-chamber parliament and a written constitution from 1958. Its motto is Liberté, égalité, fraternité: liberty, equality, brotherhood.

chapters.title: The Fifth Republic
text: Since 1792 France has had five republics, two empires and several kings. The current system, the Fifth Republic, began in 1958 when Charles de Gaulle was brought back to power during the crisis over the war in Algeria. He wanted a strong leader who could act quickly, so the new constitution gave the president much more power than before.
The constitution sets out how laws are made, what the president and parliament can do, and the rights of citizens. A Constitutional Council of nine members checks that new laws follow it.

chapters.title: President and prime minister
text: The president is elected directly by voters for five years and can serve at most two terms in a row. If no candidate wins more than half the votes in the first round, the top two face each other in a second round two weeks later.

The president lives in the Élysée Palace in Paris, leads foreign policy, commands the armed forces and controls France's nuclear weapons. They appoint the prime minister, can dissolve the National Assembly and can call referendums.

The prime minister runs the government day to day and must keep the support of the National Assembly. When the president's opponents win a majority there, the president has to pick a prime minister from the other side. This is called cohabitation, and it happened three times between 1986 and 2002.

chapters.title: Parliament
text: Parliament has two chambers. The National Assembly has 577 deputies, each elected by the voters of one area, usually in two rounds. It has the final say on most laws and can force the government to resign with a vote of no confidence.

The Senate has 348 senators. They are not elected by the public but by more than 150,000 local officials, such as mayors and councillors, so the Senate tends to speak for small towns and rural areas. It meets in the Luxembourg Palace in Paris.

highlight.title: Votes for women
highlight.text: Women in France won the right to vote in 1944 and voted for the first time in 1945, later than in many other European countries.

chapters.title: Regions, departments and communes
text: France has 18 regions: 13 in mainland Europe and 5 overseas. Regions look after things such as trains and secondary schools. Below them are 101 departments, created during the Revolution, which run social services and roads; their numbers once appeared on every car number plate.
The smallest unit is the commune. France has almost 35,000 of them, more than any other country in the EU, and each has its own mayor, from Paris to villages with fewer than 100 people.

chapters.title: Symbols of the Republic
text: The tricolour flag of blue, white and red dates from the Revolution. The national anthem, La Marseillaise, was written in 1792 as a marching song and got its name from volunteer soldiers from Marseille who sang it in Paris.

Marianne, a woman wearing a red cap, stands for the Republic. Her face appears on stamps and coins and her bust is found in every town hall. The national day is 14 July, with a military parade along the Champs-Élysées.

chapters.title: France in the world
text: France is one of the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, which means it can veto (block) the council's decisions. It is one of only a handful of countries with nuclear weapons.

It was a founding member of NATO in 1949. De Gaulle took France out of NATO's joint military command in 1966 to keep full control of its forces; it returned in 2009. France is also a founding member of what is now the European Union, and it keeps close ties with many of its former colonies, especially in Africa.

cardGroups.title: How power works

items.title: The President
items.subtitle: Elected by voters every 5 years
items.text: Leads foreign policy and the armed forces, appoints the Prime Minister and can dissolve the National Assembly.

items.title: The Prime Minister and government
items.subtitle: Appointed by the President
items.text: Run the country day to day and propose most new laws, but need the support of the National Assembly.

items.title: The National Assembly
items.subtitle: 577 deputies elected by voters every 5 years
items.text: Votes on laws and the budget, and can force the government to resign.

items.title: The Senate
items.subtitle: 348 senators chosen by local officials
items.text: Reviews and amends laws; half the senators are chosen every 3 years for 6-year terms.

items.title: The Constitutional Council
items.subtitle: 9 members appointed for 9 years
items.text: Checks that laws follow the constitution. The President and the heads of both chambers each appoint three members.

items.title: Mayors and councils
items.subtitle: Elected by local voters
items.text: Almost 35,000 communes, plus departments and regions, run local services such as schools and roads.

cardGroups.intro: Who chooses whom, and what each part of the system does.

steps.title: How a law is made
steps.intro: Most new laws follow these steps.

items.title: A bill is written
items.text: Most bills come from the government; members of parliament can propose them too.

items.title: A committee studies it
items.text: A small group of deputies or senators examines the text and suggests changes.

items.title: Both chambers debate and vote
items.text: The bill goes back and forth between the National Assembly and the Senate until they agree on the same text.

items.title: A joint committee settles disagreements
items.text: If they still disagree, 7 deputies and 7 senators try to find a compromise; if that fails, the National Assembly has the final say.

items.title: The Constitutional Council may check it
items.text: The President, the Prime Minister, the heads of either chamber or 60 deputies or senators can ask the Council to check the law.

items.title: The President signs it
items.text: The President must sign the law within 15 days, and it is published in the official journal.
